days.title: The Box and the Bottle
days.prepTonight: Dig out the twelve handprint sheets and stand them on the table. The scissors stay up out of reach. They come down in your hand three times tomorrow and go straight back. Leave the box, the bottle and the April envelope on the shelf. She gets them down herself in the morning.

opening.title: Getting Them Down Off the Shelf
opening.need: the January box · the July bottle · the April envelope · 1 chair she can stand on · 1 pen · 1 blank envelope.
steps: She drags the chair over. Stand behind her while she lifts the box down with both hands, then the bottle, and April's envelope comes off the shelf edge with them.
Read the lid out loud with her: OPEN DECEMBER 31, 2027. Then read today off the calendar. She has waited a year for this, so give her the minute.
She shakes the box and guesses what is in it. Write every guess on the blank envelope and stand it against the lid until 9:15.

main.title: Opening the January Box
materials: The April envelope, sealed since Day 92
steps: Scissors through the packing tape, yours, all the way round. She lifts the lid off and looks in before either of you reaches.
One thing out at a time, laid in a row, no digging. The photograph, the drawing, her answers, and the January walk treasure last.

Ask the four questions in the same order and write the answers word for word before she hears the old ones: favorite color, favorite food, favorite song, what she wants to do this year. Leave her grammar where it lands.
Unfold January's and read them out, then lay the sheets side by side. Read them in pairs, January's answer and then today's, and let the difference sit there.

Now the April envelope, cut open along one end with the scissors. Her spring answers go on the table between the other two, so the row reads January, April, December, and the middle set is the one she cannot remember giving.

Fresh paper and crayons, and she draws the family again with January's and April's beside her. She will tell you who she left off. Check the guesses against what came out, then photograph the table before anything moves.
main.tip: Her answers before January's. Read January's out first and she copies herself, and the copy tells you nothing.

outside.title: The Same Walk, Bare Trees Again
paras: Walk the January route the same way round and let her call every turn. The trees are back to the shape she met on the first walk of the year, bare and all structure, and she has a name for one of them. Stop where January's photograph was taken and take the fourth one from the same spot, the last of the four. Hand her a paper bag and the same instruction: one thing worth keeping. She will tell you where it is going before you do.

days.infant: Kreston is 18 months and 26 days, and on the first walk of the year he rode facing out with empty hands. He walks a good stretch of the route today and collects into his own paper bag. He has more than twenty words and box is worth handing him this morning. Give him the lid to carry and he takes the job as far as the door.

second.title: What the Bottle Was Holding
second.intro: The bottle went up beside the box in July and she asked about it again when the leaves came off. The door frame and the twelve sheets of hands follow it.
materials: The twelve handprint sheets, January through December
A long strip of paper to cut the year from
The empty shoebox, packing tape and a permanent marker
steps: The bottle holds the paper strips of July's sentences, each tied with ribbon. Scissors through the tape round the cap, yours. She tips the strips out and unties every ribbon.
Read her July strips out loud in the order she hands them over. She will not remember saying any of it, and she will argue with two.
One strip is folded, and that one is yours. She hands it over and you read it out this time.
Door frame. Shoes off, heels back, book flat on her head, pencil mark, DEC 31 beside it. Cut a strip of paper from January's line to today's and hand her both ends.
Draw round her flat hand beside January's outline, then let her put her palm inside the old one. The gap round the edge is the year.
All twelve sheets on the floor in order, January at one end and Tuesday's December at the other. Then today goes in the shoebox, taped shut, OPEN DECEMBER 31, 2028 on the lid.
second.tip: Stand the new box where the old one stood, high and in her sightline. She checked that shelf all year, and a year runs better with something on it.

alternatives: The four questions on the sofa, recorded on the phone.
Open the bottle and leave the box until tomorrow.
Lay the twelve handprints out and let her find January.
Photograph the table and put it all back unsorted.
outAgain: Playgroup, if yours runs on New Year's Eve, and many do not
A friend's house, the same one from the first week of January
The store before it shuts early, and she carries one thing for tonight
The January route once more in the last light, and ask what is different
days.krestonPM: He went on that door frame lying down on Day 1 and stands for it today, heels against the wood and your hand flat on his head. His January print sits under Azlyn's, made while somebody held his fist open. On Tuesday's December sheet he pressed his own palm down and lifted it off himself, and one sheet in the row carries a footprint.

insight.headline: She won't remember most of this year, and that isn't the point.
paras: Ask her at twenty about the tower or the bottle and you will get nothing back. Memory researchers call the gap childhood amnesia, and it takes almost everything before three or four. Her autobiographical memory is starting to hold its own contents. The rest of it went somewhere harder to point at: the words she has, the pause before she gives up on a hard thing, the assumption that an adult comes when she calls, hands that can press and tape and stir. None of it arrives with a date on it, and she cannot call it up as an episode. The year went into her. The box on the table is for you.

days.safety: The scissors open three sealed things today, so they go back up out of reach between each one and never onto the table. The January contents are choking-sized: the walk treasure, the ribbon round each strip, the sand and the stones in the bottom of the bottle. Kreston is at the table for all of it, so tip the sand into the trash yourself and the ribbons into your pocket as they come off. She is on a chair at 8:00 to reach the shelf, so keep both hands on the chair while she is up there and bring the box and the bottle down one at a time.
